utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good morning to you and your team. Are there any preliminaries you'd like to raise? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have a submission to make. My submission is that the Prosecution will object to the Defence leading evidence by the Defence expert Bilic whenever they've refer to new documents, totally new documents, to be shown to that expert. The Prosecution received a list of documents from the Defence, and those documents refer to their wish to examine them in court, bring them into court for examination by this expert. We signed the already analyst documents, however. There's also mentioning of around nine new documents not being subject to prior examination and comment by the Defence expert in his report. I submit that in these circumstances it should not be permitted for an expert to comment on new documents from the witness box. It is in violation of Rule 94 bis, and the Prosecution will be deprived of the opportunity of a Rule 94 bis expert report prior to examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who is going to address this. We haven't got a clue as to why you would like to have these witnesses [sic] put to the witness, so perhaps you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben may also be jumping the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, that's it, Your Honour. I don't know if it may be premature to explain how the witness will deal with those documents which he hasn't analysed in his report, and perhaps we can deal with that at the time. But it will be a question of a visual demonstration which the parties can themselves see as to the quality of the paper on these non-analysed exhibits and how that compares to the ones which he analysed, but not as a matter of expert opinion, more as a demonstration for the Trial Chamber and for the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. After consultation our position is as following: We have heard what you have to say, Mr. Wubben, and what you have to say -- what you had to say as well, Mr. Jones. We defer our decision to the moment when you start making use of these documents, if at all, and then we take our decision then. But we have, of course, taken into consideration what your submissions are. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I have in addition, just for clarification, yesterday we discussed the -- not calling of the other expert witness by the Defence, the military expert. I just can take it that we don't have to file now a 94 bis motion. It's just for the record, Your Honour, for later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thought we had settled that. The Defence withdrew the witness only because of the position taken by the Prosecution in requiring him present here for cross-examination and for no other reason. And then I said if I have a confirmation of that, then of course I will dispense you from having to file a motion, an ad hoc motion, in any case. It will spare you having to file a motion and us having to come down with a decision and the Defence, maybe, with a response. So that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Will you please apologise me, I have to address other business outside this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Wubben. Are there any other preliminaries from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, a brief question. For the record, I wish to state that on the list of exhibits that the Prosecutor wishes to show the witness in cross-examination, there are again P15 and P333 for which the Prosecutor has heard from the witness, Dzanan Dzananovic. These are not his signatures, and moreover the Prosecution expert said that they were most likely not Dzanan Dzanovic's signatures. I only wish to point out that these documents are persistently being shown to the witnesses in that witness's absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to respond to that? Do you wish to respond to that, Ms. Sellers, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll respond to it briefly. We're not going to anything in relationship to the signature, but moreover it's putting before the witness a bit of the contents and the chronology of events. And so we're in no way trying to mislead the witness. What I can do, if Defence counsel insist, is reconsider during break whether to show the documents at all, but there has been no intent by the Prosecution at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, I quite understand, but we have all been lawyers in our career at one time or another, and it makes a difference if you show the witness a document purportedly signed by purportedly someone they've heard of when that someone has categorically denied the paternity of the document. So if -- the reason for the purpose of your question is not to establish the paternity of the document, then I suppose you can refer to the events as they emerge from that document or those documents without showing those documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that certainly is a matter to go about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if you show me a document purportedly signed by Mr. Wubben when in actual fact it wasn't, it is one additional reason for me to take it that that is a position taken by Mr. Wubben. So -- all right. I think you've understood me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honour, I do have one other matter prior to the beginning of today's session, and that is that the Prosecution would like to hand up a new P598. P598 is a document that we were in the process - and I think I've put this on the record before - of continuing analysing the document prior to presenting it toward a witness. It has been a bit of a subject of a decision and recent decision. And the Prosecution, in reviewing the document further, realised that there were omissions of two -- well, three pages with writing on it and two pages with minimal writing and a back photocopy of a page that has nothing to do with the document. In order to be able to give to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber the document in its complete integral form, we would like to substitute P598 for what is virtually the same document, P598, but now two or three pages that had been missing are included. Also the ERN range is different, and that is how we were finally able to confirm that this was the complete integral document. I wanted to do that before today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we wish to look at that document and see what this is about, whether it's the same document, and then we can comment on it. And we wish to do so before it is replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And also once we have reached this position, which is very much understandable, I am not quite sure how wise it would be to replace one with the other when reference may have been made to the existing one, and particularly two pages carrying ERN numbers. So if eventually we come to the conclusion then that we need to have the new one in, then that will be the new one and that will be the document which we will take into account for the purpose of our deliberations later on. But I see no good reason for removing the other one from the record, for various reasons. I mean, some of which I have mentioned. The other thing I would like to mention is the following, and here I reserve the position of the Defence. I don't know what's the content of these missing pages that are now going to be present. So I'm reserving the position of the Defence if the consequence of there not having been in the records before means that they have missed some questions with some witnesses, then I have to open the doors and the windows for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely understand that. And as to your first point, I think it is correct, more logical, to not substitute the document, but possibly either give this a small A or whatever, just a new number. In addition, I will state that what we did was revise the translations and now there's another English translation that's in harmony with the complete document. As to your second point which goes to the Defence's opportunity to have redirected using this document, this document was used, I believe, on one occasion at that point, objected to the Defence did not itself use the document on redirect, but certainly the possibility lies open that they might have, had other pages been available. So I completely understand what Your Honour is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's this document, 598, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the document -- we are going down a list of different types of names with diaries. This is a document that your decision in 590 in terms of whether a witness was confronted, Adam Sedemovic [sic], I believe. It was referred to, I believe, as a war path or another type of war diary. We can christen it with a new name or baptise it with a new name. But I think when you see the document it is one that listed various brigades or units that came under Prosecution's allegation, Potocari and Pale, and showed what they did at different attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I hand this to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I would expect you to. And then I would expect feedback from the Defence, and then you are expect a decision on our part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's not likely that there will be a substitution. In other words, there will be --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I will withdraw the request for substitution and it will just be submissions. So I will hand three copies up to the Defence and that will be one copy each of translation and -- this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to this document, it was not shown to Mr. Ademovic, and that was why we objected. Mr. Ademovic testified. He's mentioned in more than one place in the document, but it was shown not to him but to other witnesses. It has been shown to more than one witness, and I wonder what the responses of those witnesses would have been to these additional pages. We do not wish the document to be tendered in this manner. It can be tendered if it's shown to some other witness, but in any case we wish to examine those pages in detail. And let me mention that we have objected to the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we would rather not have it now. We would rather have it when a decision is taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, if I can briefly state, I will concur with Madam Vidovic, and I think that that was part of the filing in one of the motions concerning the Rule 98 bis. It was not shown to Mr. Sidik Ademovic, and I believe it was stated on the record by myself that we were still in a period of analysing the document and bringing the document forward. I wish it had been in its integral form when finally it was used with witnesses, and that's why I'm being very open and placing this on the record for the Court. Now, in terms of the Defence wanting to examine the different pages, I thought it might also be relevant that if I precisely say what are the new pages so that one could go right to it. And that is the first page, page -- ERN number 02995208. You will also notice the second page as ERN number 02995208A, and that is a page that was a photocopy obviously of a back page. It has some circles and numbers on it. And then I'm informed that page that ends in ERN, I believe, 28 is also a page that was not in the previous document, so therefore we're referring to it as a new page. And then I would draw your attention, that's for the record just ERN number 02995228. And then I would draw your attention to what would be referred to as the last page with any substantial writing, and that's 02995236. So those are the four pages, one not having much writing on it, that the Prosecution would like to draw the Defence's attention to as not having been included. I would also just make it very clear on the record that this document has been disclosed in its entirety previous to this point, so these are not -- it's not new in the sense of disclosure, but only in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Translation --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And we are aware of the Defence's position on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We'll come back to this, later, after the Defence have had an opportunity to examine the document. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just say that this document was never disclosed to us in this form. Its front page did not look like this. It was not disclosed to us in the original. I wonder where these four pages have been? This is a very important and serious issue. I see Mr. Halilovic's name here and so on. Your Honours, please take into consideration this kind of behaviour by the Prosecution. What does this mean? Towards the end of our Defence case now, documents are disclosed to us in their entirety. So we have not been able to show to the witnesses who have been witnesses here and whose names are mentioned in the document, we have not been able to show them the document. Although the Prosecutor had this document, I don't know where it was. It's not just that the translation has been delivered only now; I'm sure that the front page did not look like this in the document disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may just add one matter to that. I also see immediately that on that first page and this reference to Mr. Mirzet Halilovic being commander in Pale from 4th July 1992, we had Mustafa Sacirovic here who gave a lot of evidence about what Mr. Mirzet Halilovic was doing from 1st of July, 1992 in Srebrenica itself. And absolutely that's something which I would have shown to him and dealt with him about. So I can immediately see one witness anyway who would have had to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for the Defence having raised these points. Let's make it clear on the record now that this document was disclosed in its entirety in this form, and if there has been any misunderstanding that that document in its entire form disclosed on the EDS, the Prosecution, in trying to analyse this document, had not realised that disclosure had been in its entire form and we were doing some other work product in order to secure parts of the document. The document was placed starting with ERN number 02995207. I believe that you will find that has been available in EDS. In terms of having presented this to other witnesses, it has certainly been our impression that the Defence not only objected to the document being shown to any witnesses and did not use it at that time. That I leave for any further argument, but the Prosecution felt it had an obligation to bring forward the entire document in its integral form so that it would not be seen later on that the Prosecution was disclosing documents with certain pages missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think for the moment we have to close the discussion here, and we will pick it up again later when we have more concrete information and verification. Witness, please, usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Since we started now earlier, and thanks to the indulgence of the recorder here, our plan is, unless we need to have additional breaks, to have a break at around about -- any time between 10.15 and 10.30, more likely 10.30, depending on how we stand at the time. And then of course it will be a full 30-minute break, to be followed with another break, a normal break later on, again of 30 minutes. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, good morning to you and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. We are proceeding with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to come as near as you can the microphones. That's perfect. That's fine. If in the course of your testimony you need anything, please let us know, and if at any time you feel tired or you hat a short break, we will give you a short break, as required.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance in showing the witness Prosecution Exhibit P608.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, this is purportedly a decision by the staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica dated the 12th of December, 1992, bearing the following title: List of staff members and members of the intervention platoon to receive meals in the people's kitchen. Please take a look at the document. You had occasion to review the document during proofing. Is that right? Is it right that in December 1992 there was a people's kitchen in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know of no such kitchen. There had never been any such people's kitchen in Srebrenica, let alone in 1992. There was a small kitchen run by Hakija Meholjic on the premises of Hotel Domavija. It was a small kitchen and it was held only by Hakija Meholjic. I can give you the reason. He had his own shop before the war, and when it became obvious that war would break out, he stashed the stock that was in the kitchen somewhere, and subsequently his house was torched. So it was good of him to have stored the food somewhere. Later on he relocated the -- these goods to the premises of Hotel Domavija, and this was good for many people who were able to have meals there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But isn't it true that this kitchen was set up later on?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was I believe in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please take a look at this list. Did you ever hear of any sort of intervention platoon in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of one, and I don't think one existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at the list. Under number 2, you see Osman Osmanovic. We talked about him yesterday. In December 1992, was he in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've already said, he left on the 25th of November, 1992, for Gorazde, and he could not have possibly been there on this date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the name under number 5, Smajo Mandzic. Did you know the person?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He resided in Dugo Polje and spent the entire war in Dugo Polje. He had his own group. He was a local group leader of fighters, and he was always at the front line because Dugo Polje borders with Bratunac municipality. So he never was in Srebrenica before demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the name under number 19, Hajrudin Malagic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His brother was of great assistance to me during the war. He helped me with some chores at home, he and his wife, so I know them well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, was he in Srebrenica in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. Malagic was given an assignment to take some sort of a message to Tuzla. He set out across a wooded area with a group of people, I don't know who, and he was supposed to meet up with Mirsad Mustafic in Tuzla, and Hajrudin Avdic gave him this assignment. That's why I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he asked him to set out?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in the summer of 1992. He returned only in February 1993 with a journalist, a foreigner. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please take a look at the name under number 35, Kemal Mehmedovic. Does this name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemal Mehmedovic hails from Pale. Pale was not occupied; it was free territory. So he resided at Pale throughout this period. There was no need for him to come to Srebrenica. He had a house over there, but he was quite a problematic person. I knew him from before the war. I had a friend who worked on the traffic misdemeanours court, and she would tell me that she had problems with Kemal Mehmedovic. She called him "Kemo." She said that there were numerous cases relating to him that she had to deal with. This was the misdemeanours court.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did he have anything to do with some sort of units or groups in Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of any such thing. Why would he come to Srebrenica from Pale? He had land over there. He was able to farm the land and tend to the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of 1992, were you aware of the existence of a prison in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A prison in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was never any prison in Srebrenica. There was a detention unit, especially in 1992. I find the notion of a prison being there a bit ridiculous. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after demilitarisation a prison was set up headed by Hajdin Mustafic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prison? Well, I repeat, I know only of a detention unit. I know nothing of a prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the issue of this detention you've been mentioning, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located on the premises of the public security station. It was a rather small detention unit, not a prison at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in addition to this detention unit, as you put it, which was located in the MUP building, there were some other detention premises?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this was only at a later stage in January 1993. Excuse me. I heard about this. I did not see for myself. Two or three rooms were refurbished for the purposes of detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the circumstances were that led you to come to know about these additional detention premises?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- or rather, cold at the time. And Jusufovic came to Mr. Hajrudin Avdic to inquire after the possibilities of obtaining blankets. There was no firewood, it was rather cold, and this was a wide-spread phenomenon. There was shelling. I remember that my mother sent my brother over to inquire after me because there was shelling, and he was there in my office whilst Jusufovic was waiting to be received by Avdic. We talked about this, and my brother, who was rather young at the time and is a quite sensitive man, and he said -- he proposed to go back home and bring a blanket, although he said: My mom is already angry because I already gave away everything we had. And I told him to go over to my home to bring some blankets for Nurija Jusufovic to take over to the detention unit for those people there. It was the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993. I'm afraid my emotions are interfering with my possibility to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly, Madam, if I may inquire in connection with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. If -- let's take it not just slowly, but also differently, Ms. Vidovic. Do you want a short break? If you are feeling uncomfortable -- we want to make sure that you are giving testimony with the utmost ease. So if emotionally you're feeling a little bit unhappy, we'll give you a break if you need one and have a cup of coffee and then continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not necessary at the moment. I can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we clarify a matter in order for me to ascertain whether I understood you well. You said that Mr. Nurija Jusufovic came to ask for blankets for the detention. Can you tell us for which detention premises for these blankets needed?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the additional detention premises which were made available in a house in the vicinity of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he say for whom the blankets were needed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not really ask. We presumed that they were for the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From what he told you, was it clear to you that the blankets were needed for the additional detention premises situated in this home near the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you remember, when this was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the -- it was January 1993. I recall that it was wintertime and it was rather cold.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you've just said, Nurija trying to procure blankets, were there other occasions when you talked about the provisions for the detention unit or anything in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Oftentimes they would come to see what the possibilities were to obtain firewood. We did not have any electricity, so we had to rely upon firewood, but there was no firewood in Srebrenica town so we had to go into the countryside and talk to the farmers there and try to ask them to bring firewood on carts into town, especially for the purposes of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "they," who was it who came asking for firewood?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Nurija Jusufovic. And Becir Bogilovic would come on occasion, as would Mr. Hasanovic, asking for the needs to be tended of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see these premises with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Believe me, I don't think there was any need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about who the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not interested in that. I knew what my duties were, and I did not have any spare time. I also had to take care of my family. I had underaged children, who stayed back at home, and I worried about them constantly, especially when there was shelling on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance in showing the witness Defence Exhibit D987.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document. I will read from the document. It says: "Avdic, I have here with me Serb citizens from Karno, nine of them, who are imprisoned here. They were brought in during the night, last night, and they are here now. Please decide and tell us what to do with these citizens." It is -- purportedly it is signed by Jusufovic, Nurija, commander of the SJB Srebrenica. Did you see this document before I showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The document says: "Avdic, I have those citizens imprisoned here." Based on what you knew of the contacts existing between the people there, who would be this person Avdic Jusufovic is addressing?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be Hajrudin Avdic, naturally. As Nurija Jusufovic was indeed commander of the SJB Srebrenica, it was only natural for him to address these needs to him -- or rather, to address this information to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you surprised by the fact that Nurija is addressing Mr. Avdic on this matter?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not surprised at all because I know that he was commander of the SJB, and Mr. Avdic was president of the municipal War Presidency, and of course he would address him on the issues since he was his superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone else coming to the War Presidency and discussing matters in relation to detentions -- detention units?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember Elvir Dzozic. I know him as Zele. I took some time to remember his name, but his name was Elvir Dzozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there something specific about him, something peculiar about him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lost his arm during the war. He was a decent sort of man, and I always took pity in seeing him without his arm. And he was doing his best to make sure that the detainees were doing -- were in good condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do the parties agree that there is a mistake in the English translation of document P987, that where you -- in the first line you see the word "Karm" it should be "Karno." So automatically -- the parties are agreeing that there should be a correction. And we're talking of page with ERN 0359211. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We stopped when you were talking about Zele. Do you know what Zele was doing, what his profession was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I only know that he used to come together with Nurija Jusufovic and that he was there at the detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will move to a different topic now. Were there Serb families in Srebrenica during the war?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only at the beginning of 1992. I think some five to six families stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to these Serb families, what was the position of Hajrudin Avdic and the War Presidency in relation to these Serb families?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a correct position, it was -- as far as I remember. Since Hakija Meholjic had some food under his care, they would arrange for the food to be delivered to these Serb families because there was no food to be had in Srebrenica. I remember an elderly couple who resided in the vicinity of the municipal building, and I'd go over to see them quite often to see whether they needed anything. I -- once I came to see them in -- wearing a skirt that was rather large for me. The lady asked me whether I had lost weight and I said: Yes. And I told her that all my clothes were too large for me now. And she suggested that I bring my clothes to her and that she would re-tailor them to suit me, and that was very kind of her and so I did. I recall another situation when I saw two lads I didn't know when I was on my way there. And she saw me looking at them a bit suspiciously, and she told me: Well, you know, these were refugees that were sent by the War Presidency to be put up with us, to sleep with us, and it is also good because they were worried and concerned about our safety because there were many refugees and they could also provide protection for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the War Presidency took an effort in trying to take care of these people?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We also thought that they would not target us as much if they knew that there were their people among us; however, the Serbs did not really pay much attention to this. They shelled us indiscriminately. There was this other occasion when I went over to their place and they told me most probably they ought to leave. And I told them: Why? You have your own home here, you eat the same food we eat. And they replied: Well, that's not the point. There were people from the Red Cross who came to see us and they asked that we be evacuated. I could see that they did not wish to leave, but they told me that there was this order for all the Serbs to be evacuated from Srebrenica. They were very sorry to leave their home, to leave their neighbours. We had many refugees in Srebrenica, but very few native residents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the tragedy, these families who spent some time with you in Srebrenica during the war, did they return after this tragedy?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went back to Srebrenica, I went to see this colleague of mine who works on the executions at the misdemeanours court in Srebrenica, and I inquired after this family. I forgot what their family name was because many years had passed. And so I explained to her who I was talking about, and she understood, and she said that they never wished to return, that they said that they would never return because Srebrenica was not what it once was. They are still in Serbia. And I really wanted to visit them. I would really like to see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask now that the witness be shown two photographs -- or rather, three photographs, in order to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, please look at 1 and 2. First of all, do you agree that these photographs are part of the video clip we saw yesterday showing the session of the War Presidency where you identified people?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please first look at photograph number 1 and tell us again who the people on this photograph are.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right is Aziz Nekic. To the left is Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is Hamed Alic the one with a moustache in a yellow shirt?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is Nekic the one in the blue shirt?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at photograph number 2.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is Mr. Aziz Nekic shown on this photograph as well?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's next to Hamed Alic in this photograph, too, and the one in the middle with side-burns.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who's sitting to the left of Mr. Nekic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to his other side?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdija Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Nekic is the person between Fejzic and Alic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, please, can you tell Their Honours who Mr. Aziz Nekic was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aziz Nekic worked first with Becirovic, Dzemo Becirovic. And later on he worked - and that was when humanitarian aid began to arrive - he was given the task of being chief of humanitarian aid. That was his title more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When he started working with humanitarian aid, did he have contacts with foreigners, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he had. How else could he have received humanitarian? It was foreigners who brought in humanitarian aid, and he would take it over from them, keep records of what had been received, and he would organise unloading and then the distribution of the aid at various points.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now please look at photograph number 3. Do you know the person wearing a uniform and standing to the far right of this photograph, the person with side-burns?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's Mr. Aziz Nekic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put this photo on the ELMO, please, and -- because since there is more than one person wearing a uniform and -- yes. We're talking of -- there seem to be two persons wearing a uniform, one with a cap on his head, and that's more or less the left-hand side of the photo near the person wearing the light blue jacket, and another one who is standing on the far right of the photo, right behind what appears to be another soldier wearing a metal helmet. That's the person we're talking about, the man standing behind that soldier with the metal helmet. Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aziz Nekic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a pointer, can you point to him, Madam?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness points precisely to the person on the far right of the photo, which had -- to which he had been referred to by the Bench. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you any idea how come Mr. Nekic is wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the municipal War Presidency received a few uniforms when they came from Tuzla, when the first journalist arrived by helicopter, they brought with them several uniforms. And of course Hajrudin Avdic distributed them. I think he gave one to Aziz Nekic because he was a refugee and he didn't have any clothes. Probably that's why he gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- exactly. Yes, that's what it says, as if you were reading my mind. Let's start with photo number 1, please, we'll integrate the whole thing and have it clear so that we will be sure that there are no mistakes here. Right. There are three persons that you see on this first photo. We'll start with the person on the far right wearing a yellow shirt and a moustache. Yes. Could you point to this person so that I make sure that we are referring to the same person? Could you point to that person on the photo, on the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. You are pointing at the same person I mentioned or pointed out to you. Who is that person, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now next to him in the centre of the photo, there is a person wearing a blue shirt. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Aziz Nekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he is the same person you pointed us -- pointed to us in the previous photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then there is another person at the far left of the photo wearing a black shirt and a moustache and beard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are pointing to him. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Hamdija Fejzic, the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And now, Madam Usher, could you kindly put on the ELMO photograph number 2, please. And let's start from the far right. There is a person sitting very comfortable on a sofa there, sofa-chair, in a reclined position wearing a white shirt and a kind of a gilet. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Mirsad Dudic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To his left there is a person wearing a yellow shirt with a moustache.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You're pointing to him. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to his left there is another guy with a blue shirt. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Aziz Nekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to his left, there is a person with a moustache and beard. I can't say that he is wearing a black shirt, but he seems to be holding a paper in his -- in one hand and has his other hand -- arm lifted. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Hamdija Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. She is right. And to his left there is another person with what appears to be a cream colour shirt, also holding a paper in his hand and also wearing a moustache and beard. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with this, both parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the witness can take another look at the photograph in connection with this last person.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you take another look, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Photograph number 2. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The person sitting next to Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think she is wrong, please go ahead and indicate -- suggest to her who that person is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could this be Krdzic perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. It's possible. Because both wore beards and had a similar profile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I remember yesterday --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it really is Adif Krdzic. I wasn't quite sure because I was looking at the profile. Yes, yes. It's Krdzic, Adif Krdzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the video showed Hajrudin Avdic wearing a completely different shirt, and I referred -- made a reference to the pattern of his shirt when we were describing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give these three documents a number, please. You need to help me, Madam Usher [sic], please 100 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point 1, point 2, point 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll move on to another topic. Did you know a person called Senad Alic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senad Alic, his parents and my parents had a house in the same street. They were close by. His parents lived in Germany. Senad Alic was in Germany, but he came from Germany in 1992 with a young journalist; that's how I remember him. I think the journalist's name was Philipp, but I'm not sure. He was very young and good-looking, and he was interested in everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Are you sure it was 1992 or was it 1993? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been January or February 1993. Probably February. I know it was cold. I know they sat in my office, and I made him some herb tea. And they sat and talked with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They brought uniforms from Tuzla, you said. Who was "they"? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a foreign journalist who came by helicopter. I'm not sure, but I am sure that we got two or three uniforms in the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Bosniaks who arrived as well?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Senad came to Srebrenica, what foreign language was he speaking?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His parents were in Germany, so of course he spoke German and a little English. But he spoke German well. He also spoke a little English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever come to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the only person there who could speak German and a little English, so he was used as an interpreter by the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who did he interpret for; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, sometimes for Hamdija, or anyone who needed an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll move on again. Before the war, did you have children?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take your children to the health centre in Srebrenica for check-ups?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there yourself for check-ups?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see what the medical documents looked like in that health centre before the war?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the name was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dr. Asim Cemerlic General Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any stamps of the health centre of those documents?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they bear the name Dr. Asim Cemerlic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because that was the name of the health centre and that's what it said on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This health centre, did it belong to Zvornik municipality or Srebrenica municipality? Did it have anything to do with Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Excuse me. Srebrenica was a separate municipality and Zvornik was a different municipality. There was no connection between the two. We weren't even neighbouring municipalities because Bratunac came in between.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the hospital during the war? Did it retain its name, Asim Cemerlic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was its full name?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the war it was walled the War Hospital. However, it was always, actually, called the Dr. Asim Cemerlic Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony yesterday you told us that Dr. Avdo Hasanovic was a member of the Executive Board of the municipal War Presidency. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see any documents written by him to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When he wrote reports about the epidemiological situation in the hospital and delivered them to the War Presidency, I usually saw those reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did those reports have a stamp?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a stamp on which it said "Zvornik," or did it say "Dr. Asim Cemerlic, Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Asim Cemerlic, Srebrenica. Why would it say Zvornik? The hospital was not in Zvornik but in Srebrenica, and we were Srebrenica municipality, not Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like the witness to be shown a document bearing the ERN number 01840591. This is a medical finding dated 27 December 1994, number 191/94, for the person named Avdo Huric. At the bottom of the document it says: "The finding made by Dr. Ilijaz Pilav."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at this document, primarily at the heading. And then look at the stamp. Do you see that the heading says "Srebrenica General Hospital"?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After demilitarisation, was the name changed into War Hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, the hospital was always called "general hospital." It was termed "War Hospital" simply because there was a war on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After demilitarisation, was it called again as it had been earlier?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was again called General Hospital Srebrenica, as before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the stamp affixed to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the document please be placed on the ELMO with the stamp visible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's put the original on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Further down. Is it okay? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see the name of the hospital, as contained in the stamp?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what it says?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "General Hospital, Dr. Asim Cemerlic."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the stamp you said you had seen in the reports by Dr. Avdo Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the stamp of the health care of the general hospital of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there just this one health care centre in Srebrenica which later on became the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was just this one and the same institution first called the health care centre and then the general hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document will now become Defence Exhibit D1005. It has ERN number 01840591. It consists of one page in the original, B/C/S, and another page being the English translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the usher show two Prosecution exhibits to the witness, P50 and P53. Your Honour, could P50 be placed on the ELMO first so that -- or, please, if the original could be placed on the ELMO, the B/C/S original. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, take a look at the stamp there.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this stamp says - and the document is -- dates from 1993 - there are two stamps there. Is that correct? One that was affixed across War Hospital Srebrenica and the other one next to Dr. Avdo Hasanovic's name. Please take a look at the stamps. Do you agree that the stamps say "General Hospital Zvornik, internal ward Zvornik"?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, was Srebrenica hospital ever a unit of the internal ward of the Zvornik hospital?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither before nor after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any such stamps on the reports written by Dr. Avdo Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please place the other document on the ELMO, the Bosnian original, P53.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also take a look at the stamp next to Dr. Avdo Hasanovic's name. Do you agree that this document also says "Zvornik Hospital, internal ward Zvornik"?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does the earlier comment apply to this as well?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is not the stamp of the Srebrenica General Hospital. I can't really account for this stamp here because it is not Srebrenica General Hospital's stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness be shown the document bearing the number 01838903. This is a new exhibit. I apologise. This is a report on this entry and epidemiological situation in the area of Srebrenica municipality signed by Dr. Avdo Hasanovic. The heading reads "Srebrenica General Hospital." Please take a look at this document. Please pay particular attention to the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Bosnian original be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that the document dates from July 1994; that's what the document says. Can I direct your attention to the stamp. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the stamp next to Avdo Hasanovic's name reads.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp reads 00UR health centre, Dr. Asim Cemerlic, and that's the Srebrenica stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the stamp of the Srebrenica General Hospital?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the stamp that you had occasion to see?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on reports such as this one. As I've already said, these were reports which had to do with the situation in the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding right that you used to see -- that the stamps that you used to see on Dr. Avdo Hasanovic's report are the ones such as this one?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I proceed, Your Honour, could this document be assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, Madam Vidovic, will become Defence Exhibit D1006. It consists of one page in the original B/C/S language, with ERN 01838903, and additionally two pages being the English translation thereof. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that when the court was established in July 1993 you were assigned to work there. My question is as follows: Before -- before June 1993, was there any court operational in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because there were no conditions in place for that. As I've already said, in April 1992, all intellectuals, including the judges, left Srebrenica. Srebrenica was not left with a single judge until June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to keep your answers short. We are pressed for time. Was there a court-martial ever operational in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A misdemeanours court?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the duties you were assigned to in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal War Presidency was trying to introduce an order, and their intention was to establish a lower court in Srebrenica. But we did not have the conditions for that. We did not have electricity, equipment, or eligible people. There was only Mensur Omerovic who had passed the bar exam and he was appointed president of the lower court in Srebrenica, but there weren't others with the same qualifications. We did not have the necessary equipment. We did not have a panel of judges. I think it was only at the end of 1994 that it started proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, is it right that you continued working for the court for a long time after the war?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The duties you performed at the court in 1994, did they look like anything which had to do with court work?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had some essential services that we provided, but it was just only jurists without the bar exam who were working there when they had to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under the conditions existing in Srebrenica, was it possible to conduct normal inquiries?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could conduct investigations, but only to the extent necessary. However, it was impossible to hold trials because the court did not have a panel of judges. It was only the investigative stage that could be taken care of, but only for certain cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These investigations, did they yield any information that was necessary for cases to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, hardly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any expert -- experts who had to help in the investigative stage, like the ballistics experts and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And this was one of the reasons why the court was unable to operate properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that some of the detention-related cases were sent over to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. I know that these cases were sent to Tuzla through the ham radio operators. These were detention-related cases. When detention had to be extended, this had to be done through Tuzla; however, communications with Tuzla were difficult. We had difficulties, those of us who worked at the court. Even the president of the War Presidency had difficulties. The detainees were aware of the detention period. They knew that -- for how long they could be kept in detention, and as soon as the detention orders expired, their family members would approach the War Presidency and complain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say that the cases were forwarded to Tuzla, but none of the rulings or decisions returned?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. We had enormous difficulties because the cases would be kept in Tuzla for several months, three to four months, without the decision coming back. And people complained, and rightly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that people were right in complaining, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant people who had a family member who was kept -- who was in custody, in detention. We had to wait for the decision to see whether the detention would be extended or rescinded. In the absence of such decisions, we could do nothing and there were people coming to us complaining.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did this stay the execution of cases, including the investigation and trial stages?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown a document bearing the mark DA179864. This is a record of interview of an accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at -- take a look at page 1. It says: "Record from questioning of the defendant." There below it says: "Attended by: Investigating judge." And then the record taker, Suhra Djilovic. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this document prior to your coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the person interviewed, Nezir Merdzic. Does this name ring a bell? Did you indeed work as a court reporter for this case?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I'm not sure whether this may have been retyped. I'm sure that this is not the record I typed out. I did type the record of the interview, but this is not that particular copy. For instance, take a look at the very end of the document. You have the court reporter, counsel, investigating judge, even the accused was supposed to be at the end. All of them should have been. And all of them would sign the record. Every record had to be signed by these people once it was typed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you accept that this is the document you worked on in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did type the record concerning the interview of this person, but this is not the typewritten copy I produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under the law, was it customary for all the participants in the proceedings, either before or during or after the war, to sign these documents once they were completed?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. This is customary for all the pre-trial stages. Had these documents not been signed by the court reporter, the accused, the counsel, or the investigating judge, the document would not have had any validity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, Madam Vidovic, let's make this clear. Madam, what you recall, therefore, is that in this particular case involving a certain Nezir Merdzic, you did type out a report? You do remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I remember typing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the report that you typed would then have been followed with the signatures of the various persons that would normally sign that document. In this case, yourself, defence counsel, Avdo Majstovovic [phoen], and the investigating judge, Mensur Omerovic, and you are also saying the accused or the suspect person himself. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what you are seeing here is allegedly a typed copy -- typed, unsigned copy of the original that you would have typed. Would you accept that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the end of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The end of my question is the following: Would you accept the suggestion that what you are seeing there, in front of you, in your own language, in B/C/S, is not the document that you typed out yourself and was fine -- was signed by various people, but allegedly a typed copy of it, a retyped copy of it, without signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I assert that this is only a copy, a retyped copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But -- but are you in a position to confirm to us that what appears in this document that you have been shown today, these three pages in your own language with no signatures at the end, but with an indication of various names, is a faithful reflection, reproduction, of the document that you, yourself, had signed -- had prepared and signed? Would you guarantee to us that there are no changes, no alterations in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I haven't read the text, and I couldn't know that. All I know is that as the court reporter I would always sign the record, and my signature should be on this document but I don't see it. I believe it was retyped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If I gave you time to read out this document in its entirety, do you think you would be in a position to confirm to us whether this is a faithful reproduction of the document you yourself typed out and signed, or would you still maintain that you would not be in a position to remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that every record that we made we signed in our own hand. The investigating judge, myself, and all those present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Judge Eser would like to put a question. Judge Eser, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just would like to now how it worked. Now, when there was a meeting or a hearing with a defendant and you have been there as the recorder, recording -- the record-taker, did you take notes by handwriting or did you type it directly into the machine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would type it directly on the machine, directly on the typewriter. The investigating judge would be putting questions, and I would be typing. It would be typed directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And then it would be read by the defendant, all the parties, then they would sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Everybody would read it and then sign it, especially the witness or the accused. They would certainly read it, and only then would they sign it. And then it would be signed by the investigating judge and by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: All right. This is a rather long report. Now, would this report be read to the people present or would everybody read it individually and then sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness or the accused would always read it individually. They would be given it to read, and only then would they sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And the people would stay and wait until he has read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Judge Eser. Let's give this document a number. This document, which in the original B/C/S language consists of three pages, bearing ERN DA17-9864 to 9866, and corresponding translation into English thereof, consisting of three pages, is being tendered by the Defence and marked as Defence Exhibit D1007.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this let me ask you, Madam, have you heard that trials were conducted pursuant to these investigations later on in Tuzla, and that people were acquitted because of deficiencies in the record. Have you heard of this?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of this. After the disaster that happened, I went to Tuzla. I was looking for accommodation for myself and my children. I was trying to find a school for my children. I was alone in the street with my children, and I didn't even think about these things. I had my own personal problems and obligations, so I didn't follow this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, the judge asked you: Can you tell us whether what you typed out has been correctly reproduced?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say whether everything had been faithfully reproduced from the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now. After the demilitarisation, did the situation in Srebrenica change?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't. The situation remained the same as it had been in 1992 and early 1993. The situation remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there still Serb attacks?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time. Sometimes they were even worse than before. Before the demilitarisation, we expected shelling attacks and so on, so we were careful, we were cautious. We were careful to take shelter. However, after demilitarisation we thought we could move about freely, but this was not the case. A shell would always land from somewhere, either from Tara or from Rogac. A multiple-rocket launcher would be fired once a month, for example. There was constant fear. We couldn't be safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown D551.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document. You saw it during the proofing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by Srebrenica municipality, the Presidency, from the 26th of May, 1993. And I will read to you only small excerpts in order to gain time. It says here: "Statement or communique. Srebrenica has become a large camp where there are so many problems every day that it is impossible to resolve them." Then in the third paragraph it says: "There are no free premises in Srebrenica, even the garages are full. Up to 30 people live in one small flat." And then a little lower down it says: "There is no food or electricity -- there is no water, electricity, or other living conditions in Srebrenica. When Srebrenica was declared a protected zone, three convoys would arrive every week, and now there is only one convoy with meager quantities of food. There is no food, clothes, and so on." Please turn to page 2. At the end of the second paragraph, it says: "Weekly convoys of half-empty trucks don't bring enough food for even one day." And then it goes on: "The Chetniks at their checkpoints first plunder the road convoys at their checkpoints, then tear the sacks and scatter the remaining goods around the trucks. Why do you allow this?" My question is: Does this reflect the actual situation in Srebrenica after the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This communique reflects correctly the situation in Srebrenica at the time. Everything that is stated here is how things were, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that: "About 3.000 people without a roof over their heads are spending days and nights under the open sky and we are asking for tents and sleeping bags." And please look at the end. It says that: "It's impossible to organise life in Srebrenica until the large quantities of -- large numbers of displaced persons leave. Therefore" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic, because there is a problem that I need to attend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. It's no major problem. One moment. Let's go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We left off, Madam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
