utterances.text: And my apologies to you, Madam Vidovic, for having interrupted you like this, but I thought I was duty-bound to bring this to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, we left off when I was about to refer to the organisation of life in the town. It says in this report: "It is impossible to organise life in the town until it is relieved of the burden of so many displaced persons." Please turn to the last page of the document and take a look. It says here: "In order to organise life in Srebrenica, we ask that UNPROFOR organise the sending of doctors, lawyers, and teachers to Srebrenica. We cannot agree on a demilitarisation if its sole meaning is that minimum quantities of food are delivered to the town while there is no water, electricity, telephone lines, and when schools, hospitals, courts, and other organs of civilian authority are not working. In order to make life bearable, we need cadres." Does this document reflect the actual situation in Srebrenica, especially with regard to cadres?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a huge problem. We had few literate people there, and they were working in the municipal War Presidency and the Executive Board. There were too few of them to be able to do everything. Of course we had enormous problems. We didn't have doctors, we didn't have judges, we didn't have teachers. Simply, we did not have professionals able to do things. And we had vast numbers of refugees. It was terrible. The free territory in Srebrenica was small. I regret the fact that we are short of time, otherwise I would explain certain things. It's hard for me to talk about this, but I wish I had time to describe the situation in 1993. In 1992, I've already said quite a lot about that; but in 1993 after the demilitarisation, I can say that the situation got even worse. In 1992 we still had food from the stocks that people still had, food they had stored up. In 1993, these stores ran out. Morillon came. He said we would be a protected area, and we relaxed a little. They promised us regular deliveries of humanitarian aid. They would announce seven trucks, and we would expect them happily, all the population, the refugees, we who were working. We would be looking forward to their arrival. We would be happy in the expectation of the aid. And seven trucks would arrive, four of them would be empty. Only three of them would contain food. People would see the empty trucks, and they would rush to the municipality. They would ask to see the municipal war president, and they would say: When is the food going to be distributed? Our children are hungry. They would see the seven trucks arriving, but how could we explain to them that only three of them had food in them? People didn't believe us. They said: You're stealing the food. It would have been impossible to steal it because the moment the trucks arrived, everybody would be out there in the street. They would all be rejoicing, waiting for the food to be distributed. Some people did see that the trucks were empty, and they wouldn't come. But there were lots of people who couldn't see that the trucks were empty. So we had enormous problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Madam. Thank you. And my last question to you is: Did the situation change before the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. That's how it always was. They would say humanitarian aid is arriving, 13 trucks are arriving, we would rejoice. But when they arrived, they would say: We were stopped in Bratunac and the trucks were looted. They wouldn't let them pass through. They always had problems in Bratunac or Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Vidovic. I suggest that we have the break now, and that will be a 30-minute break. And we'll take it up from there. Do you think you'll finish -- probably not, looking at your eyes. No. So our effort we laboured in vain. We came 30 minutes earlier today, but we're still not there. Don't worry. Madam, if you need to, inform your family that we will not be finishing with your testimony today. We will finish tomorrow and not today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not want to cause any false hope, but if she could maybe reserve calling her family until after we go to the next break. I will be able to judge better, in case there is a chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So rather than contacting your family now, give it another two hours, and we will know better whether you are finishing today or you're finishing tomorrow and then you can contact your family or our staff can contact your family on your behalf. Thank you. 30 minutes from now means we will start 30 minutes from now, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam, you are now going to be cross-examined by Ms. Sellers, who is one of senior counsel in the Prosecution team. You will recall what I told you the first day, yesterday, when you entered into the courtroom, that in terms of your solemn declaration you have a responsibility to answer truthfully all the questions that are put to you, irrespective of who is putting the questions. In other words, irrespective of whether it's the Defence team that is questioning you or the Prosecution team. At the end of the first break -- or the second break, rather, at 12.30, we should know more or less whether you will be here with us again tomorrow or whether you would finish the testimony -- your testimony today. And in that case, you would be able to contact your family. All right? Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'll have to say this will probably be the first time that we're using the stand and the microphone at the same time without it stretching long. So if I'm too far away from the microphone, please let me know. We're all adjusting a bit in the new courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reception on my side is perfect. I don't know about my colleagues. Are you hearing her well? And I think if there is a problem, most of the time it can be adjusted by increasing the level, the sound level. But I want to make sure that the interpreters can hear you well. All right. All right. I see thumbs up in all the booths. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, my name is Patricia Sellers. I'm standing over here; as a matter of fact, I'm the one who is standing literally now, and I'm with the Office of the Prosecution. I'll be asking you some questions, and in the interests of trying to see if we could try and conclude today, I might be going rather rapidly through some documents with you, and my intention is just to elicit testimony. It is in no way to confuse you. If you would like to slow down, take time -- more time than it appears that I'm allowing, please just let me know. There will be absolutely no problem with that, okay? I would like to begin by confirming, Ms. Djilovic, that you spent most of your adult in the town of Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know or did you know Mustafa Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what relationship, if any, he is to you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mustafa Djilovic is my husband's brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also I'd like to ask you about Ekrem Djilovic. Is he someone who's also related to you or to your husband?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ekrem Djilovic is my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And your husband and his brother, were they with you in Srebrenica during the time period of 1992 through 1994?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to some of your previous testimony, and you stated that you worked with the War Presidency, in particular Mr. Avdic, from latter part of July 1992 up until March or May 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you just confirm, was it until March 1993 or was it until May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower court was established only in May 1993, but I continued working for the municipal War Presidency because there were no conditions in place for the lower court to function, and it did not, in fact, function until the -- until the very end of 1993. I hope I made myself clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I do understand. Before you came to work for Mr. Avdic, did he have another secretary who was doing the technical secretarial work that you did?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, he did not. The municipal War Presidency was established only on the 1st of July, and I started working for the Presidency at the end of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, when you came to work for him, did you review any documents that might have been written during the month of July after the establishment of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Perhaps one or two documents, but there was no need for me to review his earlier documents unless he showed them to me personally because it had to do with something we were working on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I see. And a question that might rather common sense: I know that you had an outer office that led to Mr. Avdic's office. Well, were any papers or files that you kept that you generated, because you did quite a lot of typing yourself, was that kept in your outer office or was that kept in Mr. Avdic's office?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents were with Mr. Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So if persons came with reports or documents, then I understand that they would be handed over to Mr. Avdic. They didn't necessarily have to be handed over to you. Is that correct or am I -- have I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received documents for Mr. Avdic in his absence. Or if someone was in a hurry, had a document to hand in to Mr. Avdic but had no time to be received by him, then I would take over the document and hand it over to him later on. So this was the case only when he was absent or when he was busy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's make this clear. There are two ways of going about this matter. There are scenarios where the person, whoever it is, let's take Mr. Avdic in this case, would never really receive and keep for himself any documents, but any documents that are offered to him, he would say: Give them to my secretary. And the secretary would take those documents and then refer them to Mr. Avdic. That's one system. The other system is: You would receive some documents from individuals that you would pass on to Mr. Avdic, and Mr. Avdic would also receive some documents himself without you knowing that he has received these documents, and he would keep the entire -- the whole lot. Is this, the latter system that I have described which was in operation in Mr. Avdic's term at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I understand, so I'll repeat. In Mr. Avdic's absence, I would be the one receiving the documents for him. Naturally, upon his arrival, I would pass the documents over to him. Or when Mr. Avdic was busy and somebody came to see him or hand a document to him but Mr. Avdic was busy and the person was in a hurry, I would take the document and then pass it on to Mr. Avdic later. Have I made myself clear now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you have made yourself clear, Madam, completely clear. But there is still one aspect which has not been cleared. What if someone gave Mr. Avdic, himself, a document? Would you then -- would it also be passed on to you by Mr. Avdic or would Mr. Avdic keep it for himself? Would he inform you of the document or would he just put it on record or in his files and that's the end of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would keep the document for himself. There was no reason for him to inform me thereof. I was his subordinate; he was my superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, in other words, who was in charge of the filing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Avdic kept all the documents with himself. My office was the outer one where persons passed through. I was supposed to keep the visitors there if he was busy, and I would otherwise be typing documents when we had paper available and only in the cases when this was a matter of urgency. Because we worked in makeshift -- improvised conditions. There was a war on, and you have to understand that we had shortages of almost everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in other words, within your sphere of responsibilities, you did not have the -- the role of filing and keeping custody over these documents that were received by Mr. Avdic? That was not your responsibility, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Besides, we did not even have the material necessary for filing documents. If we happened to have the odd binder, it would be used; otherwise, there wasn't much of that around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not even have log-books to enter such information into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the second time in a day, Judge Eser and myself were thinking exactly alike. So I put the question that he meant to put. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Djilovic, for explaining this. Then the next question I would like to ask, just very briefly, has to do with Mr. Hamdija Fejzic. Did he have a secretary, a technical secretary, like yourself?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't. He didn't have a secretary. I serviced all of them, including Hamdija Fejzic, and that was in 1992 and early 1993. There was not much to do. We did not have material or conditions to enable us to work. We were there to keep this institution alive in order to make the people arriving into town and the people who were in town more comfortable, feeling that they had someone there thinking of them, taking care of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then am I correct in assuming that if there was typing to be done, then you did the typing for Mr. Fejzic and for Dzemal Becirovic, Rasid Efendic, those who were located in the same building, or is that an incorrect assumption?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be retyping, rather I'd be typing out a letter or whatever had to be typewritten. As we only had this one typewriter, we had only one ink ribbon which became worn out over time, we only used the typewriter for the essential documents, appeals or such-like writings that had to be typed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I take it that that typewriter, the functioning typewriter was on your desk or within your working area?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mechanical typewriter which was made operational. It had the ink ribbon, and it was in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And you did mention that you had to get paper. And since you were the main typist, the only typist within the municipal building, did you yourself ever go to different places to get paper so that you could type on so you could fulfil your work responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Normally all of us tried to obtain blank paper wherever we could, but this was not a specific obligation of mine. My obligation was to type whatever I was dictated, although whenever I came across some blank paper I'd bring it over to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sometime did the persons for whom you worked, Mr. Becirovic, Mr. Efendic, would they bring paper to you so that you could type some of the work or the letters that they dictated to you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They rarely dictated the text to me, but of course they would bring papers although it wasn't blank paper. Normally it was paper that had already been used on one side of the sheet, and then we'd use the blank parts of it. And this was true for the entire 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you some questions, again work-related, but concerning your schedule. You testified that you worked between the end of July until May, even a bit longer than May. Could you tell us more specifically how many times a week you would come into the office?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. It -- it all depended on the situation in the town. When shelling was more intense, I wasn't able to come into office. I'd wait for a lull in shelling. They'd tell us, you know: You should not go out when the shelling is going on. You should wait for the point when they stop to recharge their barrels and then go out. So I did not go out that often. There was a war on. The situation was dreadful. And if I were to find myself in the same situation now, I don't think I'd be able to endure it. And sometimes I wonder how I managed to endure the situation, to walk out in the street with the shells landing around me. I'd even happened to step in a puddle of blood belonging to a man who'd been hit by a shell. I did my best to help my children, the children of others. I did whatever I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, thank you. I do understand that very much that the conditions that we're speaking of were conditions that were quite difficult. Given even those very difficult conditions, could you tell the Trial Chamber that you were at the work of the municipal building once a week? Are we talking about twice a week? Are we talking about at least once a day but maybe for a very short time period? Give us an idea.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were periods when I was able to go there every day and work without a problem, and then two or three days would pass without me being able to go to work. Whenever I could, I went. There were days when I was unable to return home and had to spend the night in the cellar of the municipality building when there was heavy shelling. Those were the days when, to avoid risk, we would wait for the nightfall or spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And during that time period when you were not able to come to work, would the municipal building still be functioning? Would Mr. Avdic still receive people, receive reports, have visitors, sometimes hold meetings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know, but I think that whenever I was unable to come the gentleman was also unable to come; at least I believe so. It must have been true for everyone, that they had to remain in shelters. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Because I was going to ask you: Would you know whether that's the case for Mr. Fejzic, Mr. Becirovic, Mr. Efendic, that they conducted no business during the time periods when you were unable to come? That, if I understand correctly, you said that you do not know.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were able to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to avoid misunderstanding, which Efendic do you mean? Two different persons were mentioned, one of which did not work in Srebrenica. And when you put the question like this, it can confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm speaking about Mr. Rasid Efendic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But basically she has already answered she doesn't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, as far as I've understood -- I know Resid Efendic. I don't know Rasid Efendic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Don't bother about it. I have one question. Maybe I can close this particular parenthesis here. When you had this bombing, this -- these attacks, shelling, as you call it, were you the only person who would stay indoors and protect yourself, not go out, or was it the general practice of everyone? Everyone would stay indoors when there was shelling going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It depended on the part of town shelled. Not all of us lived in the same part of town. If the part of the town where I lived was shelled, I wouldn't go out. If the part where Fejzic and Becirovic lived was shelled, then they wouldn't come. And of course, if the entire town was being shelled, none of the people would move. It all depended on the part of town targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you cannot be more specific than that? In other words, there is no way you can tell us that there were days when you couldn't go to the municipal -- municipality building because there was shelling and that Mr. Avdic also couldn't go or Mr. Fejzic couldn't go? In other words, you're not in a position to be as specific as Ms. Sellers tried to elicit from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were days when nobody was able to come to work, but those were really rare occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Sellers, I think you have got more -- enough information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have any further questions on this, of course you can go ahead; but if not, let's close on this --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm quite satisfied with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the next organisational issue concerning your work. And is that, with the War Presidency at times there were meetings. Now, were you involved in organising the meetings, and by that I mean in contacting people who were to attend the meetings to let them know the time and the place and possibly the agenda of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That's not the way it was. I'm not sure I understand the question. Can you clarify a bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, and I appreciate you asking me that. When the meetings of the War Presidency were held, such as the one we saw on the film, was it part of your responsibility to contact the different people who were to attend the meeting? Did you tell them when the meeting would be held, what room it would be held in, the different subjects that would be discussed at the meeting? Was this part of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that as there were few people and all of them were there, it wasn't my duty to summon them, but they'd agree amongst themselves as to when the meeting should be held. And they met only when the situation permitted them to meet. It did not depend on us, in fact, on when we wanted to have the meeting. When most of the people were there, they'd discuss the possible date of the meeting. And if the circumstances permitted it, the meeting was held. You have to understand that we worked under improvised conditions. It was not a normal situation where I would be contacting people and inviting them to come for the meeting. When all these people were there, sometimes Avdic would tell them that the meeting should be held or I should -- I told them. But there were no conditions in place for the meetings to be held, as is normal; rather, depending on the circumstances, given the shelling, we met when we could. Otherwise, I would probably have been inviting people, sending a courier over to them to let them know. Since we did not have these conditions, we did not have a courier for that. We did as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And Ms. Djilovic, that's one thing I wanted to ask you. You've testified, you told the Trial Chamber there was no courier service, and yet we saw the film with a meeting that had quite a few people in the room. If I could count, there were upwards of 10 to 15 people. One of the persons came from Potocari. How was that person, if you know, notified about the meeting? Are you aware of how that happened?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that particular person happened to be in town, and some of the members of the War Presidency told the person that he or she should come to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's a possibility of what could have happened, because you don't really know how meetings or the meeting schedule was communicated to the members of the War Presidency. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I don't know. I know the ways in which they could have been notified. They could have been notified only when they were there, the situation permitting. During the morning meeting, they would discuss the possible times when they could meet. You have to know that there was a war on and the War Presidency itself was a makeshift organ which had to work under conditions which were not normal. In spite of that, there were attempts at making it work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. You've just testified that there was the morning meeting. I don't believe that I completely understand what you mean by "the morning meeting." Was this a regular occurrence, Ms. Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Rarely Hajrudin Avdic, Fejzic, sometimes Becirovic, sometimes Hasanovic, all were present to discuss their duties because they were trying to perform some of them -- those duties, and that's what I was referring to. The situation permitting, they would meet in the morning to discuss these matters, and that was when they would schedule a meeting of the municipal War Presidency. And then all of them would notify others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, the film that we saw with the meeting from the War Presidency, you were not present, physically present, in that meeting, were you, Ms. Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Usually were you present -- I'm sorry. Were you going to say something?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was sitting in my office in the room leading into the office of the president of the War Presidency. So I was sitting in the room in front.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I see. Normally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What's happening, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, my lead counsel has informed me she wasn't feeling very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why she's withdrew, but we can -- I asked her and she said we can continue for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you think that we should stop, we will also stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Hopefully it will remain in short duration, and if not, then perhaps in 10 or 15 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But do let us know, please, because I saw it happening --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- rather abruptly, so I didn't know exactly what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're quite sure that she was in the condition to confirm to you that we can proceed because if she wasn't, then obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Jones. Yes, sorry, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, no. And certainly, this is quite important.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to ask you usually or on a regular basis, did you attend the meetings of the War Presidencies -- Presidency, such as the one that we saw in the film?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not always. I did sometimes. When Mr. Avdic asked me to come in, when he needed something, only on such occasions, but that happened rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you draw up the agenda or any document that would be handed out to the participants at the meeting that would detail the subjects that were going to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I'm not aware of that. I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, let me just rephrase that. Before each meeting -- oh. Yes, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Before each meeting were you tasked with writing up an agenda, writing up a piece of paper that would have the different subjects that would be discussed at the meeting to give to participants?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We didn't have materials. I didn't have anything to write on. I didn't write any agendas. If anyone did that, it was the secretary of the municipal War Presidency, Resid Efendic. He would have done that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. And let me just ask a question that might appear quite stupid. But in lieu of not having any paper, would you inform the participants as they went into the door what would be the subject matter that would be discussed at the meeting? Would you say it orally, as opposed to giving them a written document?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Neither in writing nor orally. I have to tell you again that the situation was not normal. This wasn't normal kind of work. It was all improvised. Quite simply, no. I didn't write anything or inform anyone. They would find out at the meeting itself what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And then my other question related to the meeting in terms of your responsibilities, is that after the meeting would you be asked to write down from any notes that Mr. Avdic took a summary of the meeting or a compte-rendu?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, not always. Sometimes, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So could one --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could one say that you usually wrote down a summary of the meeting or you rarely wrote down a summary of the meeting of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never wrote any summaries, but the president would dictate something he felt necessary. He would dictate and I would type.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've mentioned -- just a couple minutes ago you testified that Mr. Efendic, Resid - I hope I'm pronouncing his name correctly - Mr. Efendic was his secretary and it was his function at the War Presidency to take down notes. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He wrote up the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, would you type the minutes after he wrote them up?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. Those minutes were not typed out. They remained as they were because we were saving paper, if we had any. We were saving it for something that it was more necessary to type out. Minutes stayed the way they were. If they were handwritten, they remained handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. Well, did you have a chance then to read over his handwritten notes, his handwritten minutes, after each meeting so that you could be kept informed of what happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I didn't type out his minutes, as I didn't type them out, there was no need. For Mr. Resid Efendic, I never typed out his minutes, so I'm not familiar with his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have another question, and again it's technical and, really, I beg your indulgence. I've never learned how to type very well, nor very fast, and I'm certain you're much -- you're very skilled at typing and taking dictation. When you type something that's being dictated to you, particularly during the time period you were at the War Presidency, did you also read back the document, understand the document, try and keep a memory of what the document was about in addition to performing the services of typing it and preserve -- memorialising it and typing?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My task was only to type what was dictated. I took care to type out what was being dictated to me as best I could, and that was my only task. I wasn't interested in the content of the text; I was looking at the letters and the esthetic appearance of the page, the layout, not the content.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in relationship to the esthetic appearance, you've testified to the Trial Chamber that on one occasion when there was bombing that someone said: Please put a heading on the paper that you were typing, and it wasn't easy for you to even say: This is one time period when I will not put a heading. So I think that shows that you are concerned about how your documents look, their appearance. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and that's what I said. The shelling then was so intense and I was so terrified that I don't even know how I managed to type that out at all, and I remember that heading very well. I didn't have time. And when he said: There's no heading. I said: Please, put it in yourself. You'll be sending this. I remember that document very well. The shelling was so intense - I explained this yesterday - that there were even grammatical errors. I was so terrified. I thought a shell might land at any moment because the Serbs shelled the municipality most often, and as my office was on the second floor I kept looking out of the window. I remember that incident really well and the dictating of that document then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As the seat of the local government, is it your opinion that the municipal building was often the recipient of probably more shelling than other places in the town?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Yes, certainly. The municipal building was shelled most often and was most subject to attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, returning a bit to esthetics, I noticed on the document that you're referring to that it appears that you might have corrected some of the spelling errors by typing over a letter in a word to make sure that it was correct, or would you just handwrite it in order to save typing paper?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the document that you typed during the bombing when someone asked you to put the heading on it.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have the time to either retype it or anything. I may have typed over a letter, but I don't think I typed over anything really because there was no time to put in corrections. I remember that day very well when we were dictating, when the gentleman was dictating that document to me. I didn't have time to go back and to type the errors over or put in handwritten corrections. I didn't even have time to put in the heading. I said: Put in the heading yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you did have time, when there was not the intense bombing of the municipal building, would you often, or on occasion, in order to save paper, write in corrections on your document by hand or possibly type over something that you had typed before?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. Under normal conditions when there would be no shelling, when it was a peaceful day - when I say "peaceful," I mean when there was no shooting - then I would be very careful when typing, to make sure that it looked nice. We were using typing appeals or reports. And I never entered corrections by hand myself, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just have a question. At this point, since different from Ms. Sellers, I have had to type quite a bit in my early days. Now, when you typed, you told us that you did not have time to re-read it and then make corrections, but sometimes it happens that while you are writing you realise that you made a mistake. Now, would you make -- would you try to correct this mistake immediately, or would you say: Leave it as it is and go on? Because you realise that you forgot a letter while typing, then would you try to correct this immediately or would you just leave it as it is and go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under normal conditions, in a normal situation without shooting, I rarely make mistakes. So I didn't need to go back, type over, or enter corrections by hand. Not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Perhaps you did not get my question completely. At least as I am used to -- sometimes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question. I don't know what document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No. I am not referring to any specific document. My question was -- my question was: As is my experience, sometimes you type, and while you are typing you realise you forgot a letter or made a wrong letter. Now, would you then try to correct this immediately or would you rather say: Leave it as it is and I'll go on? So I do not mean the situation where you have typed a letter and then you would re-read it; that's not what I mean. I mean the case where you are typing and while you are typing you realise that you made a mistake whether you would corrected it or whether you would just leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I rarely entered corrections because it was rarely necessary. I always tried to type correctly. It was an ordinary typewriter, a mechanical typewriter. Once you type over a letter you don't know what letter it actually is. So it's better to leave it as it is than to type it over. Very rarely did I type one letter over another letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Djilovic, was it ever brought to your attention that some of the persons who you typed for might have added things on to the document, either written something on the document, corrected from their point of view, a spelling of a name?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't recall. I don't know. I can't answer because I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Now, the days that you were not present at the municipal building because of the shelling, is it possible that other people used your typewriter since it was the only one in the building?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Avdic was a decent typist?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't type well, but he could have used a typewriter but he wasn't a good typist. He's a mechanical engineer, not a typist. But a brief text, yes, he could type it out. But he wouldn't do that often. He would usually write it in handwriting. There was a war on. The conditions were wartime conditions. The situation was not normal, so we didn't really feel that everything had to be typed, as would have been the case in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So if I can just try and understand what you're saying is that if Mr. Avdic wrote something out, as opposed to typing it out, that would carry the same effect? He can write something and deliver it; it doesn't have to be typed, because of the war going on?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He could have written it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, am I correct also to assume that Mr. Becirovic was not a great typist?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. Which Becirovic do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm talking -- I'm referring to Becirovic, Dzemal Becirovic, who was part of the Presidency -- I'm sorry, Dzemal Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he could type or not or what his typing was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And if you would bear with me, I would like to ask the same question --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to ask the same question in relationship to -- if you know, whether Naser Oric was a good typist.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Naser Oric so slightly. I only saw him a few times during the war. I don't know really. I'm not in a position to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he ever came over to use your typewriter, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I was the only one who had a typewriter. The only typewriter that could be used was the one in my office, and I never typed anything for Naser Oric. He never asked me to type something out for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've stated that you had the only typewriter in the municipality. And what I'd like to understand, do you mean that you had -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have the only typewriter in the municipal building, or did you have the only typewriter in the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were only two typewriters, ordinary, mechanical typewriters. I worked on one; the other one was in the office of the Executive Board. It stood there in case someone ever managed to get a ribbon for it and then it would be possible to use it. But the only mechanical typewriter that could be used was in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So am I assuming that your answer to my question is that you had the only working typewriter in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that one was in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you're really unaware if there were any other working typewriters in the municipality of Srebrenica? That's correct; right, Ms. Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- yes. I want to make sure -- Judge Eser has the same feeling I have, that she may have misunderstood your question. Perhaps you may repeat it. You could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, why don't we take it -- we'll just break it down a bit further, Ms. Djilovic. I'm to understand from your testimony - and please correct me if I am wrong - that to your knowledge you had the only working typewriter in the municipality, the opstina, of Srebrenica? Are you prepared to say that? Yes, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "the municipality of Srebrenica," I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the entire free territory? As far as I know, there was only that one typewriter, and I don't know of any other. I don't know of the existence of any other. I know that there was this one in the municipal building, and I think it was the only one that had a ribbon and that could be used in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, to your knowledge you know of your own typewriter and you don't know of any other typewriter. But you are not excluding that there could have been other typewriters with ribbons that you never came to know about? For example, are you aware whether the hospital had a typewriter? Are you aware whether the police -- the security section had a typewriter? Are you aware if Hakija Meholjic had a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at the beginning. Later on they may have managed to get a mechanical typewriter each. You know, even if you get hold of a typewriter, it would be hard to get materials, because mechanical typewriters had to have ribbons. Ribbons dry out, they get torn, they get worn out. It was very difficult to find the materials you need for a typewriter. I know by the -- my own. I'm not aware. I don't know, but I don't think they had any at the beginning at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think we can leave it at that and move forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Djilovic, thank you very much for that explanation, in particular about your working area. And I would now like to turn to a time period just very briefly before you came to work at the municipal building. In the month of June 1992, you were aware that war had broken out in the Srebrenica area. That was your testimony; correct, Ms. Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when did you become aware that the War Presidency existed and there might be a possibility of you working there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Becirovic called me to talk, when he learned I was there. He asked me to come and see him, and then I learned that there was a body called the municipal War Presidency; it was an improvised body. When he said to me "municipal War Presidency," at first I imagined something else. But when I saw what the conditions were like, it didn't look like a body or an institution. It was all makeshift. But people were doing their best. As I said yesterday, if we heard that there was a literate person somewhere, we could go and ask them to come. People were trying to set something up. It was just an attempt to do something under the conditions prevailing at the time. The town had been looted; there was nothing anywhere. When refugees arrived, all you could see for days was streets full of people, mostly women and children, people who had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, were you also aware around that same time period that there had been some attempts to organise a defence of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't start working at once. The war broke out in April, and it was only towards the end of July that I began to work. And I didn't know what was going on. I was confused. We'd all been living and working together nicely, and then suddenly those same people who had been living with us were shelling us. They had looted us. They had burnt houses. And at first I was confused. I didn't even think there was something I could do. I was just trying to survive with my children. When we went to bed at night, I would thank God that we had not been wounded and that we were still in good health. The same would happen in the morning. For days and months, I was in a state of confusion. When Becirovic asked me to come to work, I thought about it and then I said: Well, let's start. He had said to me: We have to try and do something. There are a few educated people left, a few literate people left. You see how many refugees there are. There's no one to work in the administration, to type, and you can do that. So I agreed. But when you say "defence," I don't really understand what -- can you clarify what you mean by "defence"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What were you trying to say by this word "defence"? I do apologise because I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No. Let me try and state the question a bit clearer. When I asked whether you might have been aware at some attempts to organise the defence of Srebrenica, I'm talking about an armed defence. Were you aware of any attempts of men, armed men, trying to protect Srebrenica, the town, or the outlying villages throughout the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, every village, every local commune, tried to protect its own perimeter. The -- the persons tried to defend their homes, so wherever they resided, that was the place that they tried to defend. Although, I don't know in what ways they did that because I know that we did not have any weapons and they had to prevent the Serbs from advancing into the area. I know that despite these attempts, the Serbs continued with their attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Djilovic, let me try and be even more specific. Did you hear or know about people such as Hakija Meholjic, Akif Ustic, Naser Oric, Zulfo Tursunovic prior to working at the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was not aware of this. I didn't know where these people were or what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of people such as Suljo Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Suljo Hasanovic from before the war because he also worked for the administrative organ. When I started working, I learnt that Suljo had only just arrived. He was released from a place called Suceska because he was probably in his own village when the war broke out and then subsequently came into town, when he was able to come to the town when the Serbs had already retreated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: At that time period did your husband or brother-in-law talk about men, armed men, who were trying to defend their towns or villages? Was that ever a subject of conversation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. My husband, my brother-in-law, and I were together all the time. And whatever I was unable to know, they were unable to know, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask if the witness can be shown Prosecution Exhibit P4, please. It's on Sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, I would ask you to look through this document. You will see that its date is June 15th, 1992, and it has a title: "Srebrenica TO," a number qualifying the letter. And it says: "By the powers vested in him, the commander of the Srebrenica TO, hereby issues the following order." "With the aim of confronting the aggressor and engaging in the struggle for liberation and return of the occupied territory -- occupied areas, all the commanders of self-organised armed groups are ordered to immediately commence the organisation and establishment of the Srebrenica TO units as follows." Now, you've testified that during May and June that there were local groups, people defending their own locale, and that there was Serb aggression. Would you agree with the statement in this first paragraph that talks about the aggressor and the organisation of local groups in the occupied areas?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the TO staff did not exist in May, June, or even July. As far as I understand, there was never a properly functioning TO staff in Srebrenica in the strict sense of the term.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I ask you when --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order -- or rather, had we had the army, we would have been able to have a staff. As it was, it was impossible. As for the local group leaders, when I started working I found out that there were local group leaders and that there were groups of people who got organised in the places where they lived in order to prevent the Serbs from entering the area as far as possible. That's what I know and I believe it to be true. As for this particular stamp, it's quite unclear to me. But I've told you as much as I know about this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Madam Djilovic, if I understand that your testimony is that you were just unaware? You did not know, did not speak to your relatives about any form of local organisation of an armed resistance in Srebrenica. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk about this with my family because we didn't know. I was at home at the time and I didn't know anything. Those were the days and months when we were confused. I've already said that. We were unable to believe that things were really happening that way. It was only when I started working that as I was working I learnt about the existence of local group leaders, all of whom were located in the same places where they had lived. For instance, Suceska, there was Zulfo Tursunovic, who had his local group there. He came to see Hajrudin Avdic, and that's how I got to know about it. He would talk about this group of his and how they had come under attack. As for the TO staff, it existed only before the war. I worked for the secretary for national defence, and I know what the staff of the Territorial Defence is. And I know that therefore this could not have been a proper staff. And I also find this stamp quite unclear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam -- Mrs. Djilovic, let me just -- first of all just ask you two things. We're going to have to try and keep your answers a bit shorter. Please explain fully but a bit shorter because of the time consequences. And to get more specifically to the questions that come out of the answer that you just gave, so you would agree that about 45 days after June 15th, by the end of July 1992, then you're aware of Zulfo Tursunovic having organised a group or being a local leader within Suceska, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about this when I started working.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's to say that Zulfo Tursunovic was at Suceska, that he had a group of defenders defending Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, can I also confirm that within 45 days you also learned that Naser Oric was going to be a member of the War Presidency and that his role in the War Presidency was related to the armed forces. Isn't that correct? Just --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify, please. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- I think it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which 45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can split it in two, Ms. Sellers. Always referring to these famous 45 days. And the first part would be: Would it be correct to say that within these 45 days you also learned that Naser Oric was going to be a member of the War Presidency? Answer that question first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might say that maybe it would be easier for her if I was to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: By the end of July, when you joined the War Presidency, then you learned that Naser Oric was a member of the War Presidency as a commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I found out and saw that Naser Oric was a member of the War Presidency. I did not know what his duties were and what he was doing. I only knew that he was a member of the municipal War Presidency. I didn't know what his duty was. I didn't have to know everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And then let me just continue down that vein and find out, Ms. Djilovic, if you would agree that by the end of July 1992 you then learned that Mirzet Halilovic was going to be the commander or was the commander of the military police. Is that correct? And I refer you to subsection 10(c) on the document before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm afraid that's bound to be misleading to the witness because her answer in relation to Mirzet Halilovic which she gave yesterday relates to the War Presidency. We know that this relates to a different organ. The witness has given her answers about the Territorial Defence, whether it existed. I'm afraid that her answer is going to combine what she knew about Mirzet Halilovic and the military police with this document to give the Prosecution a link between Mirzet Halilovic and the staff --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now have to ask Defence counsel, please, certain things that should not be said before the witness about as to what is the intent of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are hundred per cent correct. However, you do also need to rephrase your question because it does have the tendency to confuse the mind of the witness as to what you're really asking about Mirzet Halilovic and whether this is in connection with the works of the War Presidency and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, may I -- I mean, it is an important issue, and if need be, maybe the witness should withdraw. I am concerned that there will be by the mixture of this document and the question, there will be a spurious confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you will allow me to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please do rephrase. I think it needs to be rephrased in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Djilovic, would you please refer back to the document that's in front of you, and I would ask you to look at number 10, subsection (c). Do you see on the document it says: "At the VP" -- it says in parenthesis "firing positions. The organisation to be carried out by Mirzet Halilovic." My question to you is, did you learn by the end of July that Mirzet Halilovic was to be a commander of the military police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Can I ask for a short break, please? I'm really tired, too tired to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, I told you myself earlier on that any time you would like a break, to tell us, and I can see that you are tired.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 30-minute break starting from now. And after the 30 minutes, if you think that -- if you prefer not to proceed any further today, if you're too tired, do let us know and we'll stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know for how long it was planned to proceed. That would enable me to know how to answer your question. I don't know how many questions you have still to put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. I thought you were informed about this. We will break now for 30 minutes, that means we will start at about 10 to 1.00. And we will then stop at 1.45, quarter to 2.00. And I take it that you will not finish today?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we will resume tomorrow at 9.00, otherwise if you are feeling too tired to continue today we will stop today after the break. You will tell us: I'm too tired, we will stop, and then we continue tomorrow at 9.00. If you can continue today, I think it will be better for everyone, but I'm not trying to pressure --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to continue

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, after the witness withdraws, maybe just a minute or two to explain the objection in her absence. It might be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. I think I understand your objection, but the question is that it's through -- Ms. Sellers was right, it shouldn't be discussed in front --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Your Honour. That's why I didn't get into detail. Yes, I think Your Honour understands, but just for the record, to make it clear what my objection is. It's that this witness has given evidence about Mirzet Halilovic and the military police but that was in the context of the War Presidency. If she's shown this document which talks about the staff and then said: So can you confirm 10(c), that gives us spurious confirmation of P4 in relation to the staff when, in fact, that question is only ever related to the War Presidency. She's answered in relation to the staff, and it's, I submit, pretty clear. But if she's asked: Was Mirzet Halilovic head of the military police in the staff, it's pretty obvious what her answer is going to be given in that she's already said that there wasn't a staff in the proper sense. So I'm concerned that a misleading answer will be given. That was my objection. Also we can't overlook the fact that VP says "firing positions" in the English. And until that's -- unless and until that's clarified, then it's a complete non sequitur to read a question about firing positions and then ask about the military police. That's obviously less important, but my first submission is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be definitely confusing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I please respond, because I'm sure my learned friends are well aware that we are on cross-examination and therefore the evidence that the witness has given is being tested. Now, I think it has been established what is her position in terms of the military police as the evidence she has given so far. But it has also been established by her evidence of people who she knew was on the War Presidency when she came to join the War Presidency herself in that capacity. And I am using document P4 to ask her had she been aware of a TO staff, and her answer slowly migrated to: Well, if there was one, it was improvised, not that: Absolutely not one. I am asking her now about persons that appear on this document and then do they reappear. Does she know about them again in the capacity within the War Presidency. And I will be showing her soon a document that the Defence has used that she has confirmed when she later heard their names and positions in the War Presidency. Now, I grant you that the witness might be confused by some of my questioning and to rephrase the question. But to imply that our intent is to make her now say, yes, this document is the TO has been established, she is free to revise her answer, change her answer, maintain her answer. I would like to state, on the other hand, that, as discussed very briefly with Madam Vidovic, sometimes the witness does seem to go on with an answer, and I'm trying to not cut her off. And so she has brought up issues about this document, of what it looks like, about stamps and things. And I'm just getting a little bit concerned as to my -- am I hearing a record being played. And I don't want to bring that up in front of the witness, because I have no intent of going into certain things on the document, to keep it brief, and also to keep it relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just very briefly. I agree, it's cross-examination, but still we don't want to get misleading evidence on the record. And it was really because the question asked about Mirzet Halilovic and then

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS SAID
utterances.text: And I refer you to subsection 10(c) on the document. And so that's my concern, this linkage of her testimony with 10(c), when 10(c) has to be read in the context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it's clear enough in our minds now and we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 30-minute break, and that means we will start at five minutes to 1.00, with the proviso if she's not feeling well, I will adjourn. Thank you. And the same applies to you, Madam Vidovic. I take it that if there is a problem, we will not proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So -- now -- so [French spoken]. It has become complicated. We will not continue with any testimony this morning. I don't think I need to go into details, but there are more than one reason. I have asked the Victims and Witnesses Unit to send the witness back to the hotel, rather than bringing her to explain and whatever. However, before we adjourn, we would need a little bit your assistance on what I'm going to mention. As I hinted earlier on, we are in the process of discussing amongst ourselves and also with the registrar the appointment of a handwriting expert, one or more. Chances are that it will be one. I also remember hearing some submissions -- a submission from, actually, both of you, but mostly from the Defence, asking whether they -- you would be allowed to make submissions on terms of reference and it was also mentioned, en passant, possible nationality issues that could arise. And of course I explained, because we had anticipated all this and we had discussed it, and of course I said of course although the appointment and the terms of reference is our business and nobody else's, we agree that we only stand to gain if we received submissions on -- and we hear what your submissions are. So if you could go into these today, I'm not saying that you must, if you could, then obviously we will be utilising the minutes that we have left more profitably. The other thing is this: That one of the things that we obviously need to communicate to the would-be expert or experts - I haven't got the least clue of who this would be - is the availability of original signatures by the accused or what has been considered as original signatures by the accused. We are, of course, not in a position to turn on the Defence -- on the accused and tell him: Could you please volunteer us with a number of specimen signatures? That's of course unless he is in a generous mood and wants to come forward and gives us -- give us specimen signatures. However, from my recollection at least -- I don't know what you did in the case of Bilic, but I would take it that he had at his disposal original signatures, and I don't know what happened to those original signatures. Similarly I don't remember -- I'm being extremely honest with you, a lot of water has passed under the bridge since then, but I don't remember what Mr. Fagel, if that is his correct name, had at his disposal, and I don't remember if we have any documents where the accused's signature is undisputed. So if you could at least help us in this context -- we can find out, mind you, but the thing is if I get to the answers now it will help me try and push the registrar quicker and better.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just remind you, and I think Defence counsel can correct me if I'm misstating it, but at the very beginning of the trial that we offered under 89 (F) the affidavit of two investigators, Steve Tedder and Barney Kelly who had witnessed the actual signatures of Mr. Oric on certain those documents. And I believe there was a date that was also placed on the document. Those were the controlled copies that we used, and my recollection is that the Defence in lieu of cross-examining investigators Tedder and Kelly on their evidence of the affidavit having witness's signatures and agreed for it to be admitted as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have a vague recollection now of what you're saying, but it's a vague recollection, I must be honest. Although usually my memory is very good, I don't remember the details so I wouldn't comment. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'll address this matter of the -- of non-contentious signatures but in the spirit, as Your Honour has suggested, of making use of time. Whether I might now put on the record are concerns, submissions, et cetera, not obviously for immediate resolution nor even necessarily for response by the Prosecution because I imagine Mr. Wubben might be dealing with this. But there are -- there are four or five points which I'd like to put on record, and I understand from a brief conversation with the Chamber's Legal Officer that things are moving reasonably quickly. So I think it might be useful to do that in the course of that. I'll also mention the position from the Defence regarding non-contentious signatures. And I think I can probably group the issues into maybe six -- six categories. And I must apologise, I don't have my file in front of me, but it's fine. I can still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I've taken you by surprise, we can stop here and take it up again tomorrow so -- because I don't want either of you to be taken or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- on the wrong foot. It's certainly not my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour, and we're not taken by surprise because your Legal Officer mentioned that this would come out. It's simply that I'm not able to refer to exact P numbers. The first issue is who is appointed as the expert and that's obviously a matter for the discretion of the Trial Chamber, but we do have submissions, and at least a couple of them were going to emerge from during the course of examination of Professor Bilic. I can state now that one of them is concerned with the need for an expert to be familiar with the script in which the signatures or handwriting appear, and that's not just the question of language, Bosnian, but also Cyrillic and Latin scripts, and in the course of examination-in-chief of Professor Bilic I'll expand on why in our submission it's necessary to have someone who knows the language if they're going to carry out this forensic analysis. A second concern - I'll try not to go too quickly - is in the course of our looking for experts we noticed, or we were told by an expert from one country that if a colleague from another associated country has reached a certain conclusion, that they normally wouldn't differ from that conclusion, and that was in relation to the Dutch report. And that already posed problems for us. Again, it's an issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I can put your mind at rest on that so that you don't need to make further submissions that whoever the expert will be it will certainly not be Dutch, it will certainly not be German, at least for the time being, certainly not be Danish, and certainly not be Maltese. That's the -- the -- at least our approach. Then obviously if we are brought with our hands to the wall and there is no option but to choose a German one or a Danish one, then obviously we might go there. But for the time being that's our intention. They will be elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was less that issue. And I think since for the moment there won't be a German, it follows I can mention that we contacted a German expert whose position was basically that as they were in the same association -- professional association as the Dutch forensic examiners that they wouldn't expect to reach a different conclusion. And so our concern is that if there's someone who's from the same association as the Dutch but not Bosnian examiner, that there would already be a predisposition to agree with the Dutch expert. That raises also the question would your -- I'll say your expert for convenience, would your expert have access to the reports of the parties' experts, which is another issue? But that's as to who is appointed. The second set of issues concerns the contested sample, and I gather from the e-mail sent out by your Legal Officer that Your Honours consider that there are, I think, eight or so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Eight or nine which are contested. Our position would be that where our expert says: Probably not the signature of Naser Oric, that that is very much contested. It's a conclusion bordering on certainty, and again it's a matter which will emerge from his testimony, but saying "probably not," rather than reaching a definite conclusion is sometimes a function of whether you've got a good sample or not. It's not a function of any doubts. So we would say that actually he should look -- your expert should look at all the exhibits mentioned in our expert 's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the inclination, our inclination for the time being as well. In other words --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is the question then also of whether that includes Hamed Salihovic and Hamdija Fejzic contested signatures. But again, that's obviously a matter for you, but it's a matter which we have a position on, which is that he should see everything, and that's a submission I can expand upon at some point. In terms -- the third point would be the terms of reference, and again it's a matter for Your Honours, but we would flag up the following. Firstly, we wouldn't -- we would be concerned if your expert were to know that he was examining Prosecution Exhibits for the reason that professional and independent though he may be, there may be, conscious or unconscious, inclination to have Prosecution Exhibits from a war crimes case and to understand that they would be -- that they should find that these are genuine or that they're from the accused. Again, as I say, this isn't a fully developed submission as such, but flagging up a concern that the expert shouldn't know which way he should go, if Your Honours follow. That he has no idea what conclusion favours whom.
